E052-01.notes: Object of preposition 'of' in a relative clause requires 'whom'. 'them' creates a comma splice/run-on; 'whose' needs a following noun; 'who' is the subject case.

E052-02.notes: Original leaves 'Spending most of the 1940s on the problem' as a fragment. A comma plus participial phrase (D) attaches it correctly to Zamboni. B semicolon still leaves a fragment after it; C 'and spending' has no parallel verb to join (would need 'and spent').

E052-03.notes: 'His first successful model' is already uniquely identified, so the 'which' clause is nonrestrictive and needs a pair of commas. A (no commas) is the standard ACT wrong answer even though restrictive 'which' shows up in some edited prose; here a restrictive reading makes no sense because there is only one first model. C and D each use only one comma of the pair.

E052-04.notes: A colon after an independent clause correctly introduces the list. B: a semicolon needs an independent clause after it. C: a colon after 'such as' is an error, and 'such as' wrongly implies the list is incomplete. D is ungrammatical and awkward.

E052-05.notes: Only C quantifies the reduction (one driver versus a crew, minutes versus more than an hour) and ties back to sentence 3. The claim matches the historical record: a single operator, with resurfacing done in roughly 10-15 minutes.

flags.note: Factual overgeneralization: 'Each of the company's later models was smaller and quicker than the first' is too broad. Some later Zamboni models, such as large modern units, are not clearly smaller than the 1949 Model A. Suggested wording: 'Later models were smaller and quicker than the first' or 'Many of the company's later models...'. Also, 'the company' is never introduced in the passage.

E052-06.notes: The singular subject 'Each' takes 'was'. C adds a comma between subject and verb and keeps the plural; D keeps the plural and also shifts tense.

E052-07.notes: 'regardless of who made it' makes clear that the name is used for machines from other makers. B is a distractor about quality, and A and C have no support.

E052-08.notes: 'the figure skater Sonja Henie' is a restrictive appositive (many figure skaters exist), so it takes no commas. B's commas would wrongly imply she is the only figure skater. That is the standard ACT ruling, though some style guides tolerate B. C and D are unpaired or mismatched punctuation that splits the subject from itself. Facts are fine: Henie saw the machine at Iceland and ordered two in 1950.

E052-09.notes: 'Within a few years' follows the 1950 Henie order in sentence 8, and the widening orders lead into later models (10) and present-day fame (11). B would put the orders before any sale; C and D separate 'within a few years' from its 1950 reference point.
